record.title: On the energy landscape of the mixed even p-spin model
record.locator: Proposition 2, Theorems 4–5 and Lemma 3: zero-temperature regularity, uniqueness, control and gradient martingale.

aligned_passages.text: ### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. The support proof is conditional on a minimizer. From that hypothesis, continue directly with [the compact-strip estimates in §2.4](#strip-estimates). The construction below explains how attainment supplies the minimizer later used in the value and circuit arguments. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The coefficient classes in this comparison can be translated explicitly. In the positive-temperature convention, write $$ U_t=-\frac{\beta^2}{2}(U_{yy}+\alpha_\nu U_y^2), \qquad U(1,y)=\log\cosh y. $$ Set $\Phi_\beta(t,x)=\beta^{-1}U(t,\beta x)$ and $\gamma_\beta=\beta\alpha_\nu$. Direct differentiation gives $$ (\Phi_\beta)_t=-\tfrac12\bigl((\Phi_\beta)_{xx} +\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x^2\bigr),\qquad \Phi_\beta(1,x)=\beta^{-1}\log\cosh(\beta x). $$ Dividing the associated diffusion by $\beta$ likewise gives unit Brownian noise and drift $\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x$. Conversely, every bounded nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous coefficient on $[0,1)$ has this form: choose $\beta>0$ at least its supremum, take distribution function $\alpha_\nu=\gamma/\beta$ below one, and put the remaining probability mass at one. This identifies coefficient classes, not minimizers at different temperatures. The terminal values differ from $|x|$ by at most $(\log2)/\beta$, but passing a strict inequality to the cusp and to coefficients unbounded near one still needs uniform estimates. A qualitative crossing statement alone supplies no positive limiting fourth-moment margin. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, equation (1.2), §2 and Proposition 5.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4). Two related works sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. Several of these conditions are automatic in its density application: monotonicity supplies the one-sided bounds at a continuity point, contact on a full-support interval makes the scalar inequality an equality, and the quotient formula for the coefficient supplies stationarity. Its moment bootstrap then gives smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Appendix B, Theorem B.1 and equation (B.1), also prove strict positivity in the zero-field positive-temperature setting, where the extra noncentered-law condition is unnecessary. These results are therefore close analytic antecedents. The distinction used below is the unconditional quantitative fourth-moment margin for the comparison coefficient and its controlled passage to the zero-temperature cusp. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. The particular shifted Gaussian coefficient identity used here is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), §7][fs-cons].
